title: Discrete Random Variables
source: Dimitri P. Bertsekas and John N. Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Probability, MIT course 6.041–6.431, Fall 2000 lecture notes

steps.title: Notation
steps.objective: Read the symbols used for discrete random variables, PMFs, moments, joint models, and conditioning.

steps.title: Random variables and PMFs
steps.objective: Connect outcomes to numerical values and construct or interpret a valid PMF.

steps.title: Standard discrete distributions
steps.objective: Recognize and calculate with Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, and Poisson random variables.

steps.title: Functions of random variables
steps.objective: Find the PMF of a transformed random variable by collecting all inputs that produce each output.

steps.title: Expectation, mean, and variance
steps.objective: Compute and interpret means, moments, variances, standard deviations, and linear transformations.

steps.title: Joint PMFs and multiple variables
steps.objective: Use joint PMFs to obtain marginals, probabilities, functions, and expected values.

steps.title: Conditioning and conditional expectation
steps.objective: Condition on events or variables and use multiplication, total probability, and total expectation.

steps.title: Independence, sums, and estimation
steps.objective: Test independence and use it to analyze products, sums, binomial counts, sample means, and simulation estimates.

questions.question: X
questions.explanation: Uppercase letters such as X conventionally name random variables.

questions.question: x
options: A possible numerical value of X
questions.correct_answer: A possible numerical value of X
questions.explanation: Lowercase letters such as x conventionally denote numerical values a random variable can take.

questions.question: p_X(x)
options: The probability that X equals x
The probability that X is not x
questions.correct_answer: The probability that X equals x
questions.explanation: The PMF assigns probability mass p_X(x) to the value x.

questions.question: p_X(x) = P(X = x)
options: The definition of the PMF at x
questions.correct_answer: The definition of the PMF at x
questions.explanation: Both sides are the probability of the event that X takes the value x.

questions.question: Σ_x p_X(x) = 1
options: Every value of X has probability 1
X can take only one value
questions.explanation: The events {X = x} partition the sample space, so their probabilities sum to 1.

questions.question: P(X ∈ S) = Σ_{x ∈ S} p_X(x)
options: Multiply the masses of the values in S
Add the values in S without their probabilities
Add the masses of the values in S
questions.correct_answer: Add the masses of the values in S
questions.explanation: An event defined by a set of values is evaluated by summing the PMF over those values.

questions.question: E[X]
options: The expected value or mean of X
questions.correct_answer: The expected value or mean of X
questions.explanation: E[X] is the probability-weighted average of the possible values of X.

questions.question: E[g(X)] = Σ_x g(x)p_X(x)
options: The independence test for X and Y
The expected value rule for a function of X
questions.correct_answer: The expected value rule for a function of X
questions.explanation: The expectation of g(X) can be computed directly from the PMF of X.

questions.question: var(X)
questions.explanation: Variance measures the expected squared distance from the mean.

questions.question: σ_X = √var(X)
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance.

questions.question: var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])²
questions.explanation: Variance equals the second moment minus the square of the first moment.

questions.question: p_{X,Y}(x,y)
options: The conditional mean of X given Y
The joint PMF of X and Y
The product of X and Y
questions.correct_answer: The joint PMF of X and Y
questions.explanation: It is the probability that X = x and Y = y simultaneously.

questions.question: p_X(x) = Σ_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)
options: Marginalize the joint PMF over y
Prove X and Y are independent
questions.correct_answer: Marginalize the joint PMF over y
questions.explanation: Summing a joint PMF over all possible y values leaves the marginal PMF of X.

questions.question: p_{X|A}(x)
options: The joint PMF of X and A
The probability of A given X
The PMF of X outside A
The conditional PMF of X given event A
questions.correct_answer: The conditional PMF of X given event A
questions.explanation: The vertical bar indicates that the probability model has been conditioned on event A.

questions.question: p_{X|Y}(x|y)
options: The product of the marginal PMFs
The conditional PMF of X given Y = y
The conditional PMF of Y given X = x
questions.correct_answer: The conditional PMF of X given Y = y
questions.explanation: It describes the distribution of X after the value Y = y is known.

questions.question: E[X | Y = y]
options: The expectation of Y given X
The conditional expectation of X given Y = y
The probability that X equals y
The joint expectation of X and Y
questions.correct_answer: The conditional expectation of X given Y = y
questions.explanation: It is the mean of X calculated using the conditional PMF p_{X|Y}(x|y).

questions.question: Which statement defines a random variable?
options: A real-valued function of an experimental outcome
A probability assigned to the sample space
A list of outcomes in time order
questions.correct_answer: A real-valued function of an experimental outcome
questions.explanation: A random variable maps each outcome in the sample space to one real number.

questions.question: Which is a random variable for five coin tosses?
options: The instruction to toss five times
questions.explanation: The number of heads is numerical. A raw heads-and-tails sequence has no explicit numerical value.

questions.question: When is a random variable discrete?
options: Every outcome has the same probability
It can take only positive values
Its range is finite or countably infinite
Its range contains every real number
questions.correct_answer: Its range is finite or countably infinite
questions.explanation: Discreteness concerns the set of possible numerical values, not whether their probabilities are equal or their signs are positive.

questions.question: A point a is selected from [−1,1], and X = sgn(a). Why is X discrete?
options: Every value of a is equally likely
questions.explanation: Although the underlying outcome can vary continuously, the range of X has only three values.

questions.question: Which pair of conditions must every PMF satisfy?
questions.explanation: Probability masses are nonnegative and must sum to one across all possible values.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed and X is the number of heads. What is p_X(1)?
questions.explanation: Exactly one head occurs for HT or TH, two of the four equally likely outcomes.

questions.question: If p_X(−1)=0.2, p_X(0)=0.5, and p_X(1)=0.3, what is P(X ≥ 0)?
questions.explanation: Add the masses at 0 and 1: 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8.

questions.question: Two fair 4-sided dice are rolled and X is their maximum. What is p_X(2)?
questions.explanation: The outcomes (1,2), (2,1), and (2,2) have maximum 2, each with probability 1/16.

questions.question: A Bernoulli random variable uses which two numerical values?
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli variable encodes failure as 0 and success as 1.

questions.question: For a Bernoulli variable with success probability p, what is p_X(0)?
questions.explanation: The two outcomes exhaust the sample space, so the failure probability is 1 − p.

questions.question: Which experiment produces a binomial random variable with parameters n and p?
options: Count events in a fixed interval with rate p
Record one success or failure only
Count successes in n independent trials with success probability p
Count trials until the first success
questions.correct_answer: Count successes in n independent trials with success probability p
questions.explanation: A binomial variable counts successes across a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials.

questions.question: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of exactly two heads?
questions.explanation: There are C(3,2)=3 sequences with two heads, and each has probability 1/8.

questions.question: A geometric random variable counts:
options: Trials up to and including the first success
Successes in a fixed number of trials
Events in a fixed time interval
questions.correct_answer: Trials up to and including the first success
questions.explanation: Its possible values are 1,2,… because at least one trial is required.

questions.question: Independent trials succeed with probability 0.2. What is P(the first success occurs on trial 3)?
questions.explanation: Two failures followed by success has probability (0.8)²(0.2)=0.128.

questions.question: What is the PMF of a Poisson random variable with parameter λ?
questions.explanation: The Poisson PMF assigns mass e^(−λ)λ^k/k! to each nonnegative integer k.

questions.question: When is a Poisson(λ) model a useful approximation to Binomial(n,p)?
options: n is large, p is small, and λ=np
n is small, p is near 1, and λ=n+p
questions.correct_answer: n is large, p is small, and λ=np
questions.explanation: Rare successes across many trials lead to the Poisson approximation with the same mean np.

questions.question: If Y=g(X), how is p_Y(y) obtained from p_X?
options: Sum p_X(x) over every x with g(x)=y
Use only the smallest x with g(x)=y
Multiply p_X(x) over every x with g(x)=y
Replace every x in p_X(x) by y
questions.correct_answer: Sum p_X(x) over every x with g(x)=y
questions.explanation: All input values that map to the same output y contribute their probability mass.

questions.question: X is uniform on {−2,−1,0,1,2} and Y=|X|. What is P(Y=1)?
questions.explanation: Y=1 arises from X=−1 or X=1, so the two masses add to 2/5.

questions.question: If Y=X², which X values contribute to p_Y(9)?
questions.explanation: Both −3 and 3 square to 9, so both preimages contribute.

questions.question: If p_X(−3)=0.2 and p_X(3)=0.5, and Y=X², what is p_Y(9)?
questions.explanation: The event {Y=9} is the union of {X=−3} and {X=3}, so 0.2+0.5=0.7.

questions.question: X takes values 1,2,3 and Y=2X+1. What is the range of Y?
questions.explanation: Apply the function 2x+1 to each possible input value.

questions.question: If g is one-to-one on the range of X and y=g(x), then:
questions.explanation: A one-to-one mapping gives y exactly one preimage, so its mass is carried over unchanged.

questions.question: X has p_X(0)=0.25 and p_X(1)=0.75. If Y=5 for both X values, what is p_Y(5)?
questions.explanation: Every possible value of X maps to 5, so all probability mass is collected at Y=5.

questions.question: Why can distinct X values have the same transformed value Y=g(X)?
options: Y must have a larger range than X
A function need not be one-to-one
A PMF may contain negative values
questions.correct_answer: A function need not be one-to-one
questions.explanation: Many-to-one transformations combine the probability masses of several X values.

questions.question: X takes 0 with probability 0.4 and 10 with probability 0.6. What is E[X]?
questions.explanation: The probability-weighted average is 0(0.4)+10(0.6)=6.

questions.question: Which description best matches E[X]?
options: The most likely value of X
The probability that X is positive
A probability-weighted average of X's possible values
questions.correct_answer: A probability-weighted average of X's possible values
questions.explanation: The mean need not be a possible value or the most likely value.

questions.question: X takes −1 and 1 with equal probability. What are E[X] and E[X²]?
questions.explanation: The signs cancel in E[X], while both squared values equal 1.

questions.question: X has E[X]=3 and E[X²]=13. What is var(X)?
questions.explanation: Use var(X)=E[X²]−(E[X])²=13−9=4.

questions.question: Why is variance always nonnegative?
options: It is an expectation of squared deviations
questions.correct_answer: It is an expectation of squared deviations
questions.explanation: Each squared distance (X−E[X])² is nonnegative, so its expectation is nonnegative.

questions.question: Which measure has the same physical units as X?
questions.explanation: Variance has squared units; taking its square root restores the units of X.

questions.question: If Y=4X−3 and E[X]=2, what is E[Y]?
questions.explanation: Linearity gives E[Y]=4E[X]−3=8−3=5.

questions.question: If Y=4X−3 and var(X)=2, what is var(Y)?
questions.explanation: Adding a constant does not change variance, while scaling by 4 multiplies variance by 4².

questions.question: For a Bernoulli(p) random variable, which mean and variance are correct?
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli variable is 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise.

questions.question: X is discrete uniform on the integers from 2 through 8. What is E[X]?
questions.explanation: For a discrete uniform variable on consecutive integers a through b, the mean is (a+b)/2.

questions.question: X is discrete uniform on the integers from 2 through 8. What is var(X)?
questions.explanation: For consecutive integers a through b, var(X)=(b−a)(b−a+2)/12=(6·8)/12=4.

questions.question: For a Poisson(λ) random variable, which mean and variance are correct?
questions.explanation: Both the mean and variance of a Poisson random variable equal its parameter λ.

questions.question: A geometric random variable has success probability p=0.25. What are its mean and variance?
questions.explanation: For the trial count through first success, E[X]=1/p=4 and var(X)=(1−p)/p²=12.

questions.question: X takes −1 with probability 0.25 and 2 with probability 0.75. What is E[X²]?
questions.explanation: Use the expected value rule: E[X²]=(−1)²(0.25)+2²(0.75)=0.25+3=3.25.

questions.question: What does p_{X,Y}(x,y) equal?
questions.explanation: A joint PMF assigns probability to simultaneous pairs of values.

questions.question: What must the sum of p_{X,Y}(x,y) over all x and y equal?
questions.explanation: All possible value pairs partition the sample space.

questions.question: A joint PMF has p(0,0)=0.1, p(0,1)=0.2, p(1,0)=0.3, p(1,1)=0.4. What is p_X(1)?
questions.explanation: Sum across both Y values in the X=1 row: 0.3+0.4=0.7.

questions.question: Using the same joint PMF, what is P(X=Y)?
questions.explanation: The equal pairs are (0,0) and (1,1), with masses 0.1+0.4=0.5.

questions.question: How is E[g(X,Y)] computed from a joint PMF?
questions.explanation: Weight g(x,y) by the probability of every possible pair and add.

questions.question: Does E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] require X and Y to be independent?
options: Only if X and Y have the same PMF
Only if X and Y are Bernoulli
questions.explanation: Linearity of expectation holds for any jointly distributed X and Y.

questions.question: Let X_i indicate whether student i succeeds, with P(X_i=1)=p. For X=Σ_i X_i over n students, what is E[X]?
questions.explanation: Each indicator has mean p, and linearity gives E[X]=Σ_i E[X_i]=np.

questions.question: n people randomly retrieve hats. Let X be the number who get their own hat. What is E[X]?
questions.explanation: Each person has probability 1/n of getting their own hat; summing n indicator means gives n(1/n)=1.

questions.question: For P(A)>0, which formula gives the conditional PMF of X given A?
questions.explanation: Conditioning restricts the probability model to A and renormalizes by P(A).

questions.question: What must Σ_x p_{X|A}(x) equal?
questions.explanation: For a fixed conditioning event with positive probability, a conditional PMF is an ordinary normalized PMF.

questions.question: Which formula relates a conditional PMF to a joint PMF?
questions.explanation: The formula applies when p_Y(y)>0.

questions.question: Which multiplication rule reconstructs the joint PMF?
questions.explanation: Multiply the probability of the conditioning value by the conditional probability of X.

questions.question: Y equals 0 or 1 with probability 1/2 each. If P(X=1|Y=0)=0.2 and P(X=1|Y=1)=0.8, what is P(X=1)?
questions.explanation: Total probability gives 0.5(0.2)+0.5(0.8)=0.5.

questions.question: How is E[X|Y=y] calculated?
questions.explanation: Conditional expectation is the mean under the conditional PMF for the specified y.

questions.question: Y is equally likely to be 0 or 1. If E[X|Y=0]=2 and E[X|Y=1]=6, what is E[X]?
questions.explanation: Total expectation gives 0.5(2)+0.5(6)=4.

questions.question: For a geometric random variable counting trials until first success with success probability p, what is E[X]?
questions.explanation: After a failed first trial the process restarts, yielding E[X]=p·1+(1−p)(1+E[X])=1/p.

questions.question: X is independent of event A with P(A)>0 when:
options: X can take only one value
questions.explanation: Knowing that A occurred must leave the entire PMF of X unchanged.

questions.question: Which identity defines independence of X and Y?
questions.explanation: The joint mass must factor into the two marginal masses at every pair.

questions.question: If X and Y are independent and p_Y(y)>0, what is p_{X|Y}(x|y)?
questions.explanation: Observing Y=y gives no information about X, so its PMF does not change.

questions.question: If X and Y are independent, which expectation identity is guaranteed?
questions.explanation: Factorization of the joint PMF lets the double sum split into a product of expectations.

questions.question: If X and Y are independent, what can be said about g(X) and h(Y)?
options: They always have the same PMF
questions.explanation: Applying separate functions does not introduce interaction between independent variables.

questions.question: Which statement about conditional and unconditional independence is correct?
options: They are equivalent for every conditioning event
Neither one implies the other in general
questions.correct_answer: Neither one implies the other in general
questions.explanation: Conditioning can create or remove dependence, so each property must be checked in its own probability model.

questions.question: For any jointly distributed X and Y, which identity always holds?
questions.explanation: Means add without an independence assumption; the other identities generally require independence.

questions.question: If X and Y are independent with variances 3 and 5, what is var(X+Y)?
questions.explanation: For independent variables, the variance of a sum is the sum of variances: 3+5=8.

questions.question: X counts successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials. What is var(X)?
questions.explanation: Write X as a sum of n independent Bernoulli variables and add their variances.

questions.question: X_1,…,X_n are independent with common mean μ and variance σ². For S_n=(X_1+⋯+X_n)/n, which pair is correct?
questions.explanation: Averaging preserves the common mean while shrinking the variance by a factor of n.
